I think you could draw some sort of rough separation. Maybe mind and body aren't the best terms. But it would make sense for "body" to just be the feed-forward sensory part of the nervous system, and the "mind" to be the feed-back part that can self reflect. Of course, there is more to the body than just the nervous system, which is why the terminology isn't great.

This is a huge assertion, though, that there is only one feed-back component. I don't know any neuroanatomy, so I can't say. But the architecture could have many different chunks that are feed-back, but only have feed-forward in a tree topology, leading up to the brain as the root which can receive input from everything.

Physically there is no way to separate body from mind, nor mind or body from the surrounding environment or the rest of the universe. That's why I think if you want to make a meaningful distinction it has to be based on computational properties of the nervous system.

I think in life we can almost directly experience the extremes of mind and body. One extreme would be when you are anxiously thinking and your whole attention is on those thoughts, to the absolute exclusion of the senses. The other would be when you are totally relaxed, with very little thought, and all (mind) attention is placed on sensory input. Feeling "in your body" as they say.

Interestingly, though, all attention can be directed at just subsets of sensory input (sensory gating). So, even when you feel like you are fully "in your body" you are probably only attuned to some subset of the information coming in-- usually a subset that is relevant to what you are doing like walking or drawing or whatever. It is typically a rather narrow, task-oriented focus. But sensory gating can be modulated, with intention and practice, and with various chemicals.

With all the hype surrounding mindfulness and meditation, it's surprising how no one ever talks about sensory gating. Often I think people just practice concentration meditation-- following the breath or something like that. But learning to widen and narrow sensory gating at will is worth thinking about.

I used to be interested by psychedelic drugs, but then I learned that those states of mind are accessible without ingesting anything, and it is ultimately more fulfilling to be able to do so intentionally and with a clear head. Psychedelics still probably have a place, but I look at it as though they showed me what was possible.

I think the heart and gut in particular are almost worthy of status as specialized 2nd and 3rd brains; maybe like co-processors on your motherboard. I think that by putting one's attention on them (it seems that one can do so just by trying to attend to those regions according to your brains spatial map), you can actually stimulate their neural activity and strengthen their communication with the brain. When they say someone "has a big heart," it could quantifiably mean that over the course of their life they have put a lot of attention on their heart, and built up an intelligence and awareness of that neural subsystem. This would be an example of sensory gating again. It is pretty commonly believed that psychedelics can open up perception (reduce gating) to achieve effects as "empathogens" and so on.

There's no real reason to dismiss the idea that the heart is some sort of seat of the emotional or loving self, just because it comes up in folklore. There seems to be a bias to want to place things in the brain, which feels a little dehumanizing, and I think that might be because there is a non-negligible amount of intelligence in other parts of the body.
